result:
**Hiatus**

Somewhere in the night a house makes a sound like a knuckle cracking. Wood cooling, contracting a hair's width, releasing whatever tension the day's heat put into it. If you're awake you might sit up. If you're a child you might decide it's a person on the stairs, and lie very still, budgeting your breath, until the furnace kicks on and gives you something else to be afraid of.

Nothing was happening. That's the thing about the sound. It's the noise of a thing not doing anything, slowly, and the not-doing has a threshold, and at the threshold there's a tick.

Geologists have a word I keep returning to: *hiatus*. In a cliff face or a core sample you can read the layers like a ledger — silt, ash, limestone, the patient arithmetic of accumulation. And then sometimes two layers sit directly against each other that have no business being neighbors. Four hundred million years on the bottom, two hundred million on the top, and between them a line you could cover with a fingernail. That line is the hiatus. It means: here, for two hundred million years, either nothing was laid down, or something was laid down and then scoured off, and there is no way, from the rock itself, to tell which.

This strikes me as one of the most honest admissions any science has made. Not *we don't know what happened* but *there is no material difference, in the record, between the absence of events and the erasure of them.* The gap looks the same either way. The cliff shrugs.

I think about this because I think about my own gaps, and about how badly I want them to have been one kind rather than the other.

There are years I cannot account for. Not lost to catastrophe — that would at least be a story. Just years that failed to deposit. I know I was employed. I know I ate dinners, and some of them were probably good. I know I must have had opinions about films that came out. But the layer is thin to the point of transparency, and when I press on it looking for a specific Tuesday, my hand goes through.

The temptation is to call this waste, and I've called it that. But the geological version won't let me be so sure. Because the other possibility — that the sediment came down faithfully, day after day, and was later scoured off by something moving over it — that possibility doesn't imply the days were empty. It implies I lived them and then the record failed. The days did their work. The recording of the days is a separate technology, and it's a worse one.

Here is a thing I believe: we badly overweight the archive. We treat the unremembered as the unlived, because memory is the only instrument we have and we've forgotten it's an instrument. A thermometer that stops working doesn't make the room cold.

And yet. I don't want to be too generous about it, because there is a real difference between a life that is happening and a life that is merely elapsing, even if that difference leaves no trace. The cliff can't tell you which. But *you* were there. At the time, there was something it was like. And the not-knowing-now doesn't retroactively empty out the was-like-then; it just means you have no standing to testify.

So the question isn't *were those years good*, which is unanswerable, but something more practical: *am I currently depositing.* Is anything settling. Can I feel the silt coming down.

I notice that I can tell. Not reliably, not always, but there are days with a certain grain to them, a coarseness, where I can feel the material arriving. And there are days that are frictionless, that slide through without catching on anything, and those are the days that will not appear in the record. They're not bad days. Often they're pleasant. Frictionlessness is pleasant; that's the whole problem with it.

What creates the grain? Not intensity, I don't think. Not novelty, exactly, though novelty helps by brute force. My best guess is *difficulty of the right size*. Something you had to reach for and got, or reached for and didn't. A conversation where you said the harder true thing instead of the easier true thing. A twenty-minute stretch of genuine attention to something that didn't ask for it — a bird, a paragraph, a person's face while they're talking. Attention seems to be the binding agent. Without it the sediment doesn't consolidate; it stays suspended and washes out.

Which suggests, unfortunately, that most of what erodes my record is not tragedy but comfort. The years I can't find are not the hard years. The hard years are vivid, even when I'd rather they weren't; grief is a stratigrapher's dream, laminated, precisely dated. It's the soft years that vanish. Nothing to grip.

The house ticks again. I've been sitting here long enough for the room to cool a degree.

There's a version of this essay that ends with an exhortation — *pay attention, seize the day, notice the light on the counter.* I distrust it. Not because it's wrong but because exhortation is itself frictionless; it feels like doing something and it isn't, and you can read a hundred of them and deposit nothing.

So instead: the hiatus stays. Whatever happened in it isn't recoverable, and the two possible histories will never be distinguished, and that's not a wound, it's just the shape of the material. I have a cliff face with a line in it. Most people do. You can spend your remaining time trying to interpret the line, or you can go be the kind of thing that leaves marks.

The sound the house makes is not a person on the stairs. It never was. It's the ordinary noise of something releasing what the day put into it, and it happens whether or not anyone is awake to convert it into meaning, and tonight I was awake, and I did, and this is that — a thin layer, some silt, laid down.
